headline: AnyPS5 ports PS5 binaries to PC without emulation (87% system libraries mapped)
summary: A new tool enables automatic porting of PlayStation 5 executables to Linux and Windows, allowing native execution without a separate runtime process.
details: AnyPS5 is an innovative tool designed for automatically porting PlayStation 5 executables to Linux and Windows platforms. Crucially, it achieves this without relying on emulation or a separate runtime process, converting binaries directly to the target system's native format.

The project incorporates a relinker for executable conversion and provides implementations of system PRX libraries for dynamic linking. Its shader recompiler successfully produces SPIR-V, which is validated using Spirv-Tools when enabled.

Initial tests demonstrate promising performance, with the 2D platformer 'Dreaming Sarah' running at a stable 60 fps on modest hardware like a GTX 1050 Ti / i5-7500. The tool currently maps 87% of known PS5 system library functions, a percentage that continues to grow as more functions are declared.

AnyPS5 supports SDL-mapped game controllers, including analog sticks and triggers, and allows for keyboard and mouse controls configurable via an .ini file. The project is open-source, distributed under the GNU General Public License version 2.
caption:

topic: underdog ai assistant launches with privacy focus
headline_marked: [[Underdog launches as most private AI assistant]] yet, running fully on-device
headline: Underdog launches as most private AI assistant yet, running fully on-device
summary: Sigil Wen's Underdog AI assistant keeps user data on-device, leveraging a unique business model that avoids subscriptions and data mining, currently available for Macs and Windows PCs.
details: Sigil Wen, a Thiel Fellow and former AI hacker house resident, has launched Underdog, an invite-only beta for a highly private AI assistant. It runs entirely on-device, ensuring user data remains on their Macs and Windows PCs, with Linux, iPhone, and Android versions planned.

Underdog is powered by Husky, an inference engine built by Wen to efficiently run AI models on local hardware. This engine is designed to move less data between a computer's main and graphics chips compared to rivals, enhancing performance and privacy.

The AI assistant incorporates additional security features, including the encryption of access keys for authorized email and other user accounts. This approach aims to provide robust data protection for sensitive user information.

Underdog currently uses a 27-billion parameter reasoning model, fine-tuned from Qwen3.8-27B. Wen claims this model performs comparably to what was considered top-tier performance six months ago, like Claude Opus 4.6, for everyday tasks.

Wen emphasizes that users don't need to sacrifice privacy for capability, as the on-device model can handle common tasks such as shopping research or math homework. He anticipates these smaller models will continue to improve over time.

The business model is unique: free at first and never ad-supported. Since the AI runs on user machines, Underdog avoids high inference costs. Instead, it takes a small percentage of payment transactions made by the AI via Stripe's secure payment rails, similar to an interchange fee.

This transaction-based approach means Underdog doesn't need to mine user data, aligning its incentives with user privacy, much like a bank or credit card provider. This contrasts with many AI assistants that collect and potentially sell user data.

Conway Research, the startup behind Underdog, is backed by prominent investors including Andreessen Horowitz, Khosla Ventures, Hummingbird, SV Angel, and Stripe co-founder Patrick Collison as an angel investor.
